title: Oil Prices Dip but Hold Above $100 as Middle East Supply Threats Mount
excerpt: Brent fell to $114.60 and U.S. crude to $101.13 early Monday after a 6% weekly Brent gain, as Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities and 28 Hormuz tanker attacks this month kept the risk premium intact.
body:
• Brent crude fell $2.12, or 1.82%, to $114.60 a barrel by 0232 GMT on Monday, October 26, and U.S. crude fell $2.14, or 2.07%, to $101.13 — a dip from near six-month highs, not a reversal.
  • Prices had settled nearly $3 higher on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, leaving Brent up 6% for the week and WTI up 2.3%.
  • At least 28 vessels have been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz so far this month, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations and IMO data reported by Reuters, including at least 11 supertankers.
  • For drivers and households, the level matters more than Monday's dip: WTI above $100 and Brent above $114 keep fuel and freight costs elevated, with no supply relief yet in sight.

Oil prices dipped at the start of the week but held well above $100 a barrel, as attacks on Saudi Arabia and record tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz kept supply threats in focus. Brent crude was trading at $114.42 a barrel at the time of writing, down from over $116 last week but up from around $60 at the end of 2025, according to OilPrice.com.

West Texas Intermediate remained above $100 despite the dip from Friday's close, trading at $100.97 a barrel in OilPrice.com's snapshot, down from a 2026 high of over $112 in April but up from less than $60 at the end of December. Reuters, via The Business Standard, put the early Monday move at $114.60 for Brent and $101.13 for U.S. crude by 0232 GMT.

A dip from highs, not a change in direction

Monday's fall followed a strong end to last week. Prices had settled nearly $3 higher on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked supply concerns, with Brent finishing the week up 6% and WTI ending 2.3% higher, Reuters reported. OilPrice.com described the futures pattern as a series of climbs interspersed with declines, where the declines tend to be a lot more moderate than the climbs — a trend it called concerning if it extends, even though physical prices have eased from earlier-year highs in the past couple of weeks.

That asymmetry is why traders are not treating a $2 dip as relief. A market that falls $2 after rising $3 on Friday, and that is still roughly double its end-2025 level, is pricing a risk premium for disruption, not a return to normal supply.

Attacks continued over the weekend

The supply threat is not hypothetical. Attacks continued over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had attacked a Saudi airport and oil facilities on Saturday, Reuters reported. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The kingdom, the world's top oil exporter, restarted partial operations at its main airport on Sunday after damage in a previous round of attacks, even as the militant group vowed to keep targeting the facility.

At sea, the pressure is broader. Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations and the International Maritime Organization showed at least 28 vessels attacked in Hormuz so far this month, Reuters reported at the end of last week, with the actual number likely higher because not all attacks are reported. At least 11 targeted supertankers and damaged them — a problem in a world with tightening supply of very large crude carriers, OilPrice.com noted. Hormuz normally carries about a fifth of the world's crude and liquefied natural gas, so damage to the largest tankers tightens the fleet available for long Gulf-to-Asia voyages even when cargoes still move.

Limited offsets

Governments have used small, targeted offsets rather than a broad release. In the United States, the Department of Energy said on Friday it had authorised the release of 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery, Reuters reported — a refinery-specific fix, not a market-wide cap. Separately, Saudi Arabia will start storing crude in Singapore in the second half of 2027 to strengthen the resilience of its supply chain in the region, energy ministers from both countries said on Monday. That helps future resilience; it does not add barrels this week.

What to watch

The next signals are traffic, not talk: whether tanker transits through Hormuz hold up after a record month of attacks, whether Houthi strikes on Saudi facilities resume after Sunday's interceptions, and whether inventory and freight data show the supertanker shortage easing. Until those turn, every dip is likely to be bought against the same fear that drove Friday's close — that the next attack removes supply faster than any reserve release can replace it. For oil-importing economies including India, and for U.S. households facing fuel prices set off a $100-plus benchmark, that keeps inflation pressure alive even on a down day.
